extracted.intended_audience: fantasy and science fiction writers / fiction writers interested in immersive world-building
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating immersive fictional worlds—especially in fantasy and science fiction—by using sensory detail, everyday-life elements, and consistency to pull readers into the setting without heavy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage the Senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging the senses is a powerful way to pull your readers into your story. The challenge is to use these details without making it feel like 20 pages of setting description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy sensory details naturally through character experience; use techniques such as placing a character in a new place or removing a sense to highlight others. Examples referenced: The Pendragon Series, Bobiverse, All the Light We Cannot See. Balance is important—use vivid sensory anchors but avoid long expository passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight
rubrics_metrics.description: The way your character interprets what they see tells the reader so much about the world. Setting elements like architecture, clothing, and terrain offer chances to build the character’s voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe what the character notices (and fails to notice) to indicate what is normal or abnormal in the world. Use visual detail to enrich the story and to foreshadow or reveal character perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound is subjective and one of the hardest senses to convey because readers will map unfamiliar sounds to known ones quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simile and metaphor to translate alien or unfamiliar noises into comparisons the character would make (e.g., magic might sound like a lawn mower or a horde of angry bees). Let sound convey more than raw noise—use it to imply culture, danger, or mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell & Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Smell and taste (food, incense, nature, garbage) convey culture and create strong, lasting associations for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use food and scent to signal cultural differences (e.g., bland post-apocalyptic rations vs vibrant portal-fantasy cuisine). Evocative, concrete descriptions can produce visceral reactions in readers and anchor memory of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch covers textures, weather, and norms of physical affection; it can be used heavily but often unconsciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on simile and metaphor to describe tactile experiences; doing so both tells what the character feels and what their reference points are in the world (e.g., 'his skin felt as dry and rough as concrete').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Character Perspective to Filter Sensory Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory descriptions should be filtered through a character’s background and perspective so comparisons make sense to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose similes/metaphors and reference points that align with the character’s experience. This anchors the world to the character and maintains internal logic (e.g., an Earth-raised protagonist will compare unknown things to familiar Earth items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques: Fish-out-of-Water & Sensory Deprivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two effective techniques for exploring senses are: (1) moving a character from a familiar place to a new one, and (2) removing one of a character’s senses so others become heightened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both approaches justify extensive sensory exploration (the protagonist experiences everything as new) and can also create obstacles or threats. Examples: portal fantasy protagonists and characters lacking sight (All the Light We Cannot See).

rubrics_metrics.name: Populate with Everyday Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Make worlds feel real by filling them with everyday people and activities—bystander reactions, non-plot-essential characters, and mundane tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include rituals and systems (eating habits, schooling, commerce, waste management, local labor like mail or trash collection) to add texture. Small mundane details can show whether people are connected or disconnected from aspects of their society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in Sensory Details and World Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency is key: sensory details and world rules should remain internally coherent across the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contradictory descriptions (e.g., describing the same object two different ways). Prevent anachronisms or modern phrasing that breaks immersion. Use searches for modern words, keep notes, and rely on beta readers to catch inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, Don't Tell — Reveal Through Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should infer world elements from context and character observations rather than from long expository blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer revealing information organically through scenes and reactions; heavy exposition is generally discouraged (except perhaps in some epic genres). Let readers build the world in their minds—when your description conflicts with their mental image, immersion can break.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Earth-Specific References That Break the World
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use Earth-specific references that wouldn’t fit the technology level or culture of your fictional world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit for phrases or objects that feel out of place (e.g., engines, brakes screeching, toilet flushing in a medieval-feeling fantasy). Replace or rephrase to match the world’s level of technology and idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing Exercise Constraints and Post-Write Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice exercise: write a 500-word scene of an alien marketplace using all five senses and everyday-life elements, with a protagonist new to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While writing: focus on sight, sound, smell/taste, touch, and mundane activities; show the character’s reactions; use comparisons appropriate to the character; avoid Earth-specific references; maintain consistency; reveal via context. After writing: highlight each sensory detail in different colors, ensure all five senses are present, and expand one detail to show how it reflects broader culture or technology.
